cards.statement: An LCP of 2.5 seconds falls within the good range.
cards.explanation: The good LCP boundary includes 2.5 seconds. Values above 4 seconds fall in the poor range.

source.title: Defining the Core Web Vitals metrics thresholds

cards.statement: Core Web Vitals assessment uses the median page-load experience.
cards.explanation: Core Web Vitals assessment uses the 75th percentile, which exposes slower experiences that a median can hide.
cards.misconception: The middle observation determines the assessment.

source.title: Defining the Core Web Vitals metrics thresholds

cards.statement: Core Web Vitals assessment pools mobile and desktop visits.
cards.explanation: Core Web Vitals assessment evaluates mobile and desktop page loads separately.
cards.misconception: A combined device sample determines the assessment.

cards.statement: web.dev accepts two good Core Web Vitals out of three as a pass.
cards.explanation: web.dev says tools should award a pass when all three Core Web Vitals meet their good targets.
cards.misconception: The general pass rule permits one metric to miss its target.

cards.statement: INP assesses responsiveness throughout a page visit.
cards.explanation: INP observes responsiveness over the visit, so interactions well after loading remain relevant.

cards.statement: Pending Web Vitals have a scheduled transition toward Stable status.
cards.explanation: Pending metrics have passed initial testing and feedback, with a timeline set for promotion to Stable.

cards.statement: Stable Web Vitals remain open to definition improvements.
cards.explanation: Stable means established guidance and support, not a frozen definition; corrections and improvements remain possible.

cards.statement: Navigation TTFB starts after service worker startup completes.
cards.explanation: Navigation TTFB includes service worker startup when a worker participates in the navigation, so initialization contributes to the measured wait.
cards.misconception: Service worker initialization occurs outside navigation TTFB.

cards.statement: Painting a plain CSS background color can trigger FCP.
cards.explanation: A plain background-color paint can mark First Paint, but FCP waits for content such as text or an image.
cards.misconception: Any nonblank paint qualifies as contentful.

cards.statement: Waiting for a web font can delay FCP on a text-first page.
cards.explanation: When font loading holds back the first visible text, that wait contributes to the time before FCP.

cards.statement: The Chrome UX Report includes browsing experiences collected from Microsoft Edge.
cards.explanation: CrUX collects eligible Chrome experiences; sharing the Chromium engine does not make Edge data eligible.
cards.misconception: CrUX aggregates data from any Chromium-based browser.
cards.volatilityNote: CrUX browser and platform eligibility can change.

cards.statement: An eligible CrUX origin includes experiences on pages that lack page-level CrUX data.
cards.explanation: Origin aggregation includes eligible user experiences across its pages, even when individual pages fail page-level eligibility.

cards.statement: The CrUX API groups its current field performance measurements into calendar-month reporting periods.
cards.explanation: The CrUX API reports a rolling 28-day collection period, rather than a fixed calendar-month period.
cards.misconception: The API uses fixed monthly reporting periods.

cards.statement: PageSpeed Insights displays available origin field data when page-level data is insufficient.
cards.explanation: PageSpeed Insights falls back to available origin data when a URL lacks enough CrUX samples for page-level reporting.

cards.statement: PageSpeed Insights accepts good LCP and CLS for a pass when INP data is insufficient.
cards.explanation: With insufficient INP data, PageSpeed Insights bases its pass assessment on good LCP and CLS at the 75th percentile.

cards.statement: A typical lab page-load test starts with a returning visitor's populated browser cache.
cards.explanation: Lab tests typically start with a cold cache, whereas returning visitors in field data may reuse cached resources.
cards.misconception: A standard lab load simulates a repeat visitor with cached assets.

source.title: Why lab and field data can be different (and what to do about it)

cards.statement: Lighthouse's page-load CLS result includes shifts caused by scrolling through the page.
cards.explanation: A load-only lab run sees shifts during loading, not the later browsing activity captured by field measurements.
cards.misconception: A page-load lab result covers the rest of a real visit.

source.title: Why lab and field data can be different (and what to do about it)

cards.statement: Local INP in Chrome DevTools reflects the interactions performed during the test.
cards.explanation: A DevTools local INP result characterizes the interactions exercised in that test, rather than a population of real visits.

cards.statement: A good TBT result establishes that real users also experience good INP.
cards.explanation: TBT is a useful lab proxy for INP, but a good TBT result does not establish good real-user INP.
cards.misconception: A proxy metric proves the corresponding real-user result.

cards.statement: LargestContentfulPaint has Baseline support across the major browser engines.
cards.explanation: MDN marks LargestContentfulPaint as Baseline 2025, newly available across current browsers since December 2025.
cards.volatilityNote: Baseline maturity and browser compatibility can change; older browsers may lack this API.

cards.statement: LayoutShift has Baseline support across the major browser engines.
cards.explanation: MDN marks LayoutShift as experimental and not Baseline because support remains limited.
cards.misconception: LayoutShift has the same cross-engine availability as established performance APIs.
cards.volatilityNote: LayoutShift implementation and Baseline status can change.

cards.statement: An inline SVG made of vector paths can qualify as an LCP image candidate.
cards.explanation: LCP considers an image element inside SVG, rather than treating a vector-only SVG drawing as an image candidate.
cards.misconception: Inline SVG vector drawings qualify like embedded raster images.

cards.statement: LCP considers CSS url() background images as possible candidates for the largest element.
cards.explanation: LCP image candidates include elements whose CSS backgrounds load images through url().

cards.statement: A video's first displayed frame supplies its LCP timing when it arrives before the poster.
cards.explanation: For video, LCP uses the earlier of the poster image load time and the first frame presentation time.

cards.statement: A large visible heading is eligible to become a page's LCP element.
cards.explanation: LCP considers block-level elements containing text, so a large heading or paragraph can be the candidate.

cards.statement: Chromium treats a background image covering the entire viewport as an eligible LCP candidate.
cards.explanation: Chromium excludes full-viewport elements as a heuristic for filtering backgrounds rather than main content.
cards.misconception: The largest possible visible background automatically qualifies.
cards.volatilityNote: Browser LCP candidate-filtering heuristics can change.

cards.statement: CSS upscaling makes an LCP image's reported area larger than the image's intrinsic area.
cards.explanation: LCP compensates for image upscaling, so CSS enlargement does not let the reported area exceed the image's intrinsic area.
cards.misconception: CSS enlargement increases measured image size beyond its intrinsic dimensions.

cards.statement: LCP counts a text block's CSS padding as part of its candidate area.
cards.explanation: LCP sizes text using the bounds of its text nodes, excluding CSS padding, borders, and margins.
cards.misconception: LCP measures the decorated CSS box rather than the text area.

cards.statement: Rendering a larger eligible candidate causes the LCP API to emit a new entry.
cards.explanation: The LCP API reports successive record-size candidates as they render, rather than reporting just one initial candidate.

cards.statement: Removing the LCP candidate from the DOM leaves its earlier qualifying paint in the record.
cards.explanation: Removing an element does not undo its earlier qualifying paint or erase its candidacy from LCP reporting.

cards.statement: The LCP API continues selecting new candidates after the user starts scrolling.
cards.explanation: LCP candidate reporting stops at user input such as scrolling; later renders do not extend that load measurement.
cards.misconception: LCP keeps following content as the user scrolls.

cards.statement: Google's LCP tools exclude visits whose page load starts in a background tab.
cards.explanation: Background-tab loads are excluded from LCP because timing them would not represent a visible loading experience.

cards.statement: A parent page's LargestContentfulPaint entries include candidates rendered inside its iframes.
cards.explanation: The LCP metric includes iframe content, but the parent page's API entries do not expose those iframe candidates.
cards.misconception: Top-level API entries cover descendant browsing contexts.

cards.statement: The LCP sub-part timeline starts when the browser receives the first HTML byte.
cards.explanation: The LCP breakdown includes TTFB, beginning when navigation starts rather than when the HTML response arrives.
cards.misconception: Time before the HTML response sits outside the LCP breakdown.

cards.statement: web.dev measures LCP resource load delay from TTFB until the LCP resource request starts.
cards.explanation: Resource load delay captures the gap before the browser begins fetching the LCP resource.

cards.statement: LCP resource load duration covers the wait to display an image after its download finishes.
cards.explanation: Waiting after the LCP resource finishes loading belongs to element render delay, not resource load duration.
cards.misconception: The resource loading phase continues until the browser paints the image.

cards.statement: A text LCP element using a system font has zero resource load delay and duration.
cards.explanation: System-font text needs no LCP resource download, so both resource-loading sub-parts are zero.

cards.statement: web.dev suggests allocating roughly 40% of the overall LCP time to resource load duration.
cards.explanation: The suggested breakdown allocates about 40% to resource loading; it is an optimization target, not a required ratio.

cards.statement: The preload scanner discovers an LCP image URL stored inside an external JavaScript bundle.
cards.explanation: The preload scanner scans HTML, not JavaScript source. An image URL in the initial HTML is discoverable before application code runs.
cards.misconception: The preload scanner extracts asset URLs from application JavaScript.

cards.statement: web.dev recommends lazy-loading the LCP image to reduce loading contention.
cards.explanation: web.dev explicitly advises against lazy-loading the LCP image because it delays discovery and loading of critical content.
cards.misconception: General lazy-loading advice also applies to the LCP image.

cards.statement: In Chrome, fetchpriority="high" gives an LCP image high priority from its initial request.
cards.explanation: Chrome starts an image marked fetchpriority="high" at high priority instead of waiting for layout to promote it.
cards.volatilityNote: Chrome can change its resource-priority implementation.

source.title: Optimize resource loading with the Fetch Priority API

cards.statement: Preloading a CSS background LCP image lets its request start before the stylesheet reveals its URL.
cards.explanation: An HTML preload exposes a CSS background image early, bypassing the stylesheet-discovery dependency.

source.title: Preload critical assets to improve loading speed

cards.statement: The Layout Instability API compares visible elements' starting positions across successive rendered frames.
cards.explanation: The Layout Instability API detects displacement of already visible content, such as a paragraph pushed downward by a newly inserted banner.

cards.statement: The browser multiplies impact fraction by distance fraction to calculate a layout shift's score.
cards.explanation: A layout shift's score combines its impact fraction and distance fraction by multiplication, so both factors affect its contribution.

cards.statement: CLS adds together the scores of separate session windows over the full page visit.
cards.explanation: CLS takes the highest-scoring session window, rather than adding scores from separate windows together.
cards.misconception: The cumulative score spans separate bursts of shifts across the entire visit.

cards.statement: LayoutShift.hadRecentInput flags shifts that follow a qualifying input by less than 500 milliseconds.
cards.explanation: LayoutShift.hadRecentInput identifies shifts close to qualifying user input, allowing those expected shifts to be excluded from CLS.

cards.statement: A LayoutShift entry's sources list identifies the element responsible for causing the movement.
cards.explanation: LayoutShift.sources lists elements that moved; their movement may instead originate from another element being inserted or resized.
cards.misconception: Layout shift attribution identifies the root cause rather than the affected elements.

cards.statement: Animating an element with transform: translate() contributes that element's movement to CLS.
cards.explanation: Movement produced by transform: translate() does not trigger layout shifts and therefore does not contribute to CLS.
cards.misconception: Visible movement from a CSS transform is scored like a layout-position change.

cards.statement: The CLS metric includes layout shifts that happen inside embedded iframes.
cards.explanation: CLS includes iframe shifts, but a parent page's layout-shift entries omit shifts inside its frames.

cards.statement: The browser derives an image's initial aspect ratio from its HTML width and height attributes.
cards.explanation: Image width and height attributes supply an initial aspect ratio, allowing the browser to reserve space before image loading finishes.

cards.statement: Impact fraction measures the area newly exposed by an element's movement, relative to the viewport.
cards.explanation: Impact fraction uses the union of unstable elements' visible areas before and after movement, divided by viewport area.
cards.misconception: Impact fraction counts newly exposed space instead of the combined old and new areas.

cards.statement: Distance fraction compares a shift's travel distance with the moving element's own largest dimension.
cards.explanation: Distance fraction divides the greatest horizontal or vertical movement by the viewport's largest dimension, not the element's.
cards.misconception: The moving element's size provides the denominator for distance fraction.

cards.statement: INP includes the browser's response to continuous scrolling among its measured interactions.
cards.explanation: INP measures click, tap, and keyboard interactions; continuous scrolling is outside its scope.
cards.misconception: INP treats continuous scrolling as a qualifying interaction.

cards.statement: INP omits one additional slowest interaction for every 50 interactions during a page visit.
cards.explanation: For interaction-heavy visits, INP drops one highest-latency result per 50 interactions, then uses the worst remaining result.

cards.statement: The INP metric includes interactions with controls inside embedded iframes.
cards.explanation: INP includes iframe interactions, although a parent page's Event Timing entries do not expose interactions inside its frames.

cards.statement: INP assigns a zero value to a page visit spent entirely in passive viewing.
cards.explanation: A visit with no qualifying interactions has no INP value; missing interaction data is not a zero-latency result.
cards.misconception: A visit with no interaction supplies a perfect numerical INP result.

cards.statement: INP finishes timing an interaction when the browser completes its event handlers.
cards.explanation: INP also includes presentation delay after the callbacks, lasting until the browser can present the next frame.
cards.misconception: Completing the interaction's JavaScript callbacks ends the measured latency.

cards.statement: The blocking period of a long task consists of the portion extending beyond its first 50 milliseconds.
cards.explanation: A long task's blocking period excludes its first 50 milliseconds, even though the task occupies the main thread throughout.

cards.statement: In Chrome, scheduler.yield() favors continuation work over new tasks at the same priority.
cards.explanation: After scheduler.yield(), continuation work gets a boost over ordinary tasks at the same priority; higher-priority work can still run first.
cards.volatilityNote: scheduler.yield() support and scheduling implementations can evolve.

cards.statement: Repeated nested setTimeout(..., 0) calls keep the browser's effective minimum delay at zero.
cards.explanation: Browsers impose a positive minimum delay after enough nested timeouts, so repeatedly yielding with a zero timeout can introduce extra waits.
cards.misconception: A zero timeout argument bypasses the minimum delay imposed on nested timers.

cards.statement: Grouping layout reads before style writes reduces repeated forced layout calculations.
cards.explanation: Batching layout reads before writes avoids repeatedly making the browser recalculate geometry after successive style changes.

source.title: Avoid large, complex layouts and layout thrashing

cards.statement: content-visibility: auto reduces rendering work by removing offscreen elements from the DOM.
cards.explanation: content-visibility: auto skips rendering work for eligible offscreen content while keeping that content in the DOM.
cards.misconception: Skipping offscreen rendering shrinks the document's DOM tree.

source.title: How large DOM sizes affect interactivity, and what you can do about it

cards.statement: In Chrome, the Long Animation Frames API requires a task over 50 ms before it reports a slow frame.
cards.explanation: A long animation frame can contain several shorter tasks; the Long Animation Frames API detects frame-level delays that task-only measurement can miss.
cards.misconception: A long animation frame requires an individually long task.
cards.volatilityNote: Long Animation Frames API support remains browser-dependent and may expand.

cards.statement: The browser waits until a stylesheet is completely parsed before it uses that CSSOM to build the render tree.
cards.explanation: Later CSS rules can override earlier ones, so MDN says the CSSOM is used for the render tree only once fully parsed, while DOM construction is incremental.

cards.statement: An element with display: none keeps a layout box in the browser's render tree.
cards.explanation: display: none excludes the element and its descendants from the render tree, so they occupy no layout space.
cards.misconception: Hiding an element with display: none retains its layout box.

cards.statement: The HTML parser continues past a stylesheet link while the browser downloads the stylesheet.
cards.explanation: A stylesheet download does not itself pause HTML parsing; the parser can continue constructing the document.

cards.statement: A print stylesheet linked with media="print" blocks the initial rendering of a page on screen.
cards.explanation: A stylesheet whose media query does not match the current display is not render-blocking for that display.
cards.misconception: A linked stylesheet blocks rendering even when its media condition does not match.

cards.statement: The browser executes async scripts in the order their tags appear in the HTML.
cards.explanation: External async scripts execute when ready, so their order can differ from their order in the HTML.
cards.misconception: async preserves document order for script execution.

cards.statement: Module scripts defer execution until HTML parsing finishes by default.
cards.explanation: The browser's default module-script behavior waits for document parsing to finish before evaluation.

cards.statement: The defer attribute postpones an inline classic script until the browser finishes parsing HTML.
cards.explanation: Browsers ignore defer on inline classic scripts; adding it does not postpone their execution.
cards.misconception: defer controls inline classic scripts in the same way as external classic scripts.

cards.statement: In Chrome, blocking="render" lets an async body script become explicitly render-blocking.
cards.explanation: Chrome honors blocking="render" for scripts in the head; the attribute does not make an async body script explicitly render-blocking.
cards.misconception: Explicit render blocking works on scripts regardless of their position in the document.
cards.volatilityNote: Support for blocking="render" differs between browser engines and can change.

cards.statement: A click handler can use import() to defer loading feature code until the user requests it.
cards.explanation: Calling import() when a feature is requested moves its module loading off the initial startup path.

cards.statement: A preconnect hint can shorten connection setup for resources hosted on the document's own origin.
cards.explanation: preconnect provides no same-origin benefit because the connection to the document's origin is already open.
cards.misconception: A page needs another connection warm-up for its own origin's subresources.

cards.statement: A preload link with as="script" executes the script as soon as the browser finishes fetching it.
cards.explanation: Preloading a script fetches it for later use; the preload link does not execute the downloaded code.
cards.misconception: Fetching a script through preload also triggers its execution.

cards.statement: A preload link uses imagesrcset and imagesizes to choose an image for the current viewport.
cards.explanation: Responsive image preloads use imagesrcset and imagesizes to select the appropriate candidate before an img element requests it.

cards.statement: modulepreload prepares a JavaScript module by parsing and compiling it ahead of its execution.
cards.explanation: modulepreload places the prepared module in the document's module map, reducing processing needed when it is later used.

cards.statement: The HTML Standard requires modulepreload to fetch the target module's dependencies.
cards.explanation: The HTML Standard makes fetching dependencies an optional optimization when the browser processes modulepreload.
cards.misconception: Preloading a module obligates the browser to preload its dependency graph.

cards.statement: A prefetch hint prepares a resource for a navigation the user is likely to make next.
cards.explanation: prefetch targets likely future use, allowing the browser to fetch a resource before the user reaches the page that needs it.

source.title: Assist the browser with resource hints

cards.statement: fetchpriority="high" fixes a request's priority at the same level across browser engines.
cards.explanation: fetchpriority is a relative hint; the browser determines its effect on internal resource scheduling.
cards.misconception: The same fetchpriority value dictates an identical internal priority across engines.

cards.statement: The fetchpriority attribute changes request priority when placed on an iframe element.
cards.explanation: HTML defines fetchpriority for img, link, and script elements, not iframe elements.
cards.misconception: iframe accepts fetchpriority as an operative loading attribute.

cards.statement: fetch() accepts a priority option for adjusting the relative priority of its request.
cards.explanation: The priority option passed to fetch() expresses a preference relative to other requests of the same type.

cards.statement: Preload schedules secondary resources for periods when critical downloads leave bandwidth idle.
cards.explanation: Preloads compete with critical requests for bandwidth; overuse can slow loading instead of waiting for spare capacity.
cards.misconception: Preload waits for unused bandwidth before fetching secondary resources.

source.title: Assist the browser with resource hints

cards.statement: WebP supports alpha-channel transparency alongside lossy image compression.
cards.explanation: Lossy WebP can preserve an alpha channel, so a transparent image does not require lossless encoding.

cards.statement: A progressive JPEG shows its top part at full quality before its lower part appears during download.
cards.explanation: That describes a baseline JPEG. A progressive JPEG shows the entire image at once, blurry at first, and each scan sharpens it as the transfer continues.
cards.misconception: Progressive loading means the image fills in from the top at full detail.

cards.statement: MDN describes PNG compression as retaining the pixel information encoded in the image.
cards.explanation: PNG compression retains the pixel data it encodes; reducing file size through compression does not discard that information.

source.title: Image file type and format guide

cards.statement: The browser selects the smallest supported-format file among a picture element's sources.
cards.explanation: A picture element uses the first source whose type and media conditions match. It does not compare the file sizes of matching sources.
cards.misconception: The browser chooses among picture sources by comparing download sizes.

cards.statement: Omitting sizes makes the browser infer a srcset source size from the image's CSS width.
cards.explanation: For width-descriptor selection, an omitted sizes attribute defaults to 100vw, the viewport width, rather than the image's computed CSS width.
cards.misconception: The browser measures the CSS layout width when sizes is omitted.

cards.statement: With width descriptors in srcset, the browser adds src as a 1x image candidate.
cards.explanation: With density descriptors, src can supply a 1x candidate; width-based srcset makes the browser ignore src.
cards.misconception: src enters the candidate set regardless of descriptor type.

cards.statement: decoding="async" hints that the browser can paint other content ahead of image decoding.
cards.explanation: Asynchronous decoding expresses a preference to present other content first, rather than hold its next paint for the image to decode.

cards.statement: The browser applies loading="lazy" to ordinary img elements by default.
cards.explanation: An img element defaults to eager loading, which fetches the image regardless of its distance from the viewport.
cards.misconception: Native image loading automatically defers offscreen images.

source.title: Browser-level image lazy loading for the web

cards.statement: The browser waits for layout to locate an image before applying loading="lazy".
cards.explanation: Native image lazy loading needs the image's layout position to decide when its request should begin.

source.title: Lazy load images and iframe elements

cards.statement: Native image lazy loading can defer requests while the browser's JavaScript setting is disabled.
cards.explanation: Browsers defer native lazy-image requests only when JavaScript is enabled; disabling scripting preserves ordinary image loading.
cards.misconception: Native deferral works identically with scripting enabled or disabled.

cards.statement: During the font block period, the browser removes the waiting text from layout calculations.
cards.explanation: During the block period, the browser lays out text using an invisible fallback font; the text still occupies space.
cards.misconception: Invisible text during font loading has no layout footprint.

source.title: CSS Fonts Module Level 4: Font Display Timeline

cards.statement: Under font-display: block, the browser shows fallback text if the web font is still loading after the block period.
cards.explanation: block gives a short block period and an infinite swap period: text stays invisible only briefly, then a fallback font shows it until the web font arrives and swaps in.

cards.statement: font-display: optional can replace visible fallback text with a web font that arrives late.
cards.explanation: The optional strategy has no swap period. A font that misses its brief block period leaves the fallback in use for that visit.
cards.misconception: optional permits a late replacement after fallback text appears.

cards.statement: WOFF2 uses Brotli compression to reduce the amount of font data a browser downloads.
cards.explanation: Brotli compression helps WOFF2 deliver font data in smaller files than WOFF, reducing transfer work.

cards.statement: Preloading a font requires crossorigin even when the font URL shares the page's origin.
cards.explanation: Font fetches use CORS mode. The preload needs crossorigin to match that mode even for a font served from the same origin.

cards.statement: The browser starts a font download when it first parses that font's @font-face declaration.
cards.explanation: An @font-face declaration alone does not request its file; normal CSS font loading starts when page styling uses the face.
cards.misconception: Declaring a font face starts its download immediately.

cards.statement: web.dev cites Web Almanac data in which sites using third-party fonts rendered faster than self-hosting sites.
cards.explanation: web.dev says the Web Almanac saw faster renders with third-party fonts and that self-hosted fonts are much less likely to win without a CDN and HTTP/2.

cards.statement: With unicode-range, the browser downloads the matching glyphs of a font as a partial file.
cards.explanation: unicode-range decides whether a font face is needed: MDN says if the page uses one character in the range, the whole font is downloaded. Byte savings come from separate subset files.
cards.misconception: The descriptor makes the browser download part of an individual font file.

cards.statement: line-gap-override replaces the CSS line-height value on elements using that font.
cards.explanation: line-gap-override changes the font face's line-gap metric used in line layout; it does not replace an element's CSS line-height declaration.
cards.misconception: A font metric descriptor overwrites an element's line-height declaration.

cards.statement: A response's max-age freshness period starts when the browser receives the response.
cards.explanation: max-age counts from response generation at the origin. An Age header reduces the freshness time remaining when the browser receives it.
cards.misconception: Receipt by the browser restarts the freshness clock.

cards.statement: A shared cache uses s-maxage ahead of max-age when a response carries both directives.
cards.explanation: s-maxage overrides max-age for shared-cache freshness, letting servers give shared caches a separate lifetime.

cards.statement: A cache treats Cache-Control: no-cache as a ban on storing the response.
cards.explanation: no-cache permits storage but requires validation before reuse; it controls reuse rather than forbidding storage.
cards.misconception: no-cache prohibits storage instead of requiring revalidation.

cards.statement: The must-revalidate directive triggers validation while the cached response remains fresh.
cards.explanation: must-revalidate permits reuse while a response is fresh. Once stale, the cache must validate it before reuse.
cards.misconception: must-revalidate forces validation even during freshness.

cards.statement: A server responds with 304 when a conditional GET's If-None-Match matches the current ETag.
cards.explanation: For an unchanged representation, the server sends 304 Not Modified with no body, allowing the client to reuse its stored response.

cards.statement: Replacing a file at the same URL on the server makes the browser refetch it while its cached copy is still fresh.
cards.explanation: The browser reuses a cached response until it is no longer fresh. web.dev puts a fingerprint or version in the file name, so changed content gets a new URL.
cards.misconception: Changing a file on the server invalidates a browser's fresh cached copy.

source.title: Prevent unnecessary network requests with the HTTP Cache

cards.statement: Vary: Accept-Encoding adds the request's Accept-Encoding value to cache variant selection.
cards.explanation: A cache distinguishes responses using the named request header, preventing reuse of a variant for an incompatible encoding preference.

cards.statement: A client advertises the compression formats it accepts in a Content-Encoding request header.
cards.explanation: Content-Encoding identifies the coding applied to a representation. Accept-Encoding communicates the client's acceptable codings.
cards.misconception: Content-Encoding advertises the client's decoding preferences.

cards.statement: A gzip response's Content-Length describes the body's byte count after decompression.
cards.explanation: For an encoded body, Content-Length refers to the encoded bytes sent, rather than the larger decoded representation.
cards.misconception: Content-Length reports the size of the original uncompressed content.

cards.statement: Transfer-Encoding describes message transfer between neighboring HTTP nodes.
cards.explanation: Transfer-Encoding applies to an individual network hop, so intermediaries may use different transfer encodings on successive hops.

cards.statement: The browser reconstructs a page's JavaScript heap during a bfcache restore.
cards.explanation: A bfcache restore resumes the saved document and JavaScript heap instead of rebuilding the runtime from cached resource files.
cards.misconception: A bfcache restore recreates the document's runtime.

cards.statement: The browser sets pageshow.persisted to true when it restores a page from the bfcache.
cards.explanation: The persisted flag on pageshow distinguishes a restored document from an ordinary page load.

cards.statement: pagehide.persisted=true confirms successful bfcache storage by the browser.
cards.explanation: pagehide.persisted=true signals an intent to cache the page, rather than a guarantee of a later restore.
cards.misconception: Intent to cache guarantees a future restore.

cards.statement: web.dev recommends pagehide in place of unload for page-exit handling.
cards.explanation: web.dev advises avoiding unload and using pagehide for exit handling, including bfcache transitions.

cards.statement: MDN recommends keeping a beforeunload listener after the user saves pending edits.
cards.explanation: MDN recommends attaching beforeunload while unsaved changes exist and removing the listener when that warning is no longer needed.
cards.misconception: A permanent beforeunload listener is recommended for saved pages.

cards.statement: web.dev treats a page whose window.opener is non-null as a safe candidate for the bfcache.
cards.explanation: web.dev says a page with a non-null window.opener can't safely enter the bfcache, because pages trying to access it could break; rel="noopener" avoids creating the reference.
cards.misconception: Opener references between windows have no effect on bfcache eligibility.

cards.statement: In Chrome, a page served with Cache-Control: no-store can qualify for the bfcache.
cards.explanation: Chrome permits no-store pages under extra restrictions and evicts them when cookies or other authorization methods change.
cards.volatilityNote: Chrome's eligibility restrictions and eviction conditions for no-store pages can change.

cards.statement: Chrome exposes cross-origin iframe blocking details through its notRestoredReasons API.
cards.explanation: For cross-origin frames, Chrome masks the detailed reasons; the top-level report can include a masked reason instead.
cards.misconception: The parent page receives cross-origin iframe diagnostics in full.
cards.volatilityNote: Browser support and the details exposed by notRestoredReasons can change.

cards.statement: web.dev recommends resetting INP to zero when a page returns from the bfcache.
cards.explanation: A restore begins a distinct visit for INP measurement, so earlier interaction latencies should not carry into the restored visit.

cards.statement: freeze and resume are Baseline lifecycle events across major browser engines.
cards.explanation: freeze and resume remain Chromium-specific lifecycle events, rather than Baseline features.
cards.misconception: The lifecycle events have cross-engine Baseline availability.
